entry.title: Who Runs This Blog
entry.content:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم، 

الحمد لله والصلاة والسلام على رسول الله

I am a Salafī seeker of knowledge, following the methodology of the Salaf as-Ṣāliḥ in understanding the Qurʾān and Sunnah — free from blind following of any school, and free from the leniency of those who dilute the texts to suit the times.

My path began independently. I was drawn early to the works of Shaykh al-Albānī, whose approach grounded my thinking. I studied books like Ibn Ḥazm's al-Muḥallā, and especially this one, for its disciplined argumentation and rigorous use of evidence. Over time, I came to understand that sound knowledge requires not only reading texts, but understanding how the Salaf themselves understood and lived them — so I invested heavily in that. I especially read Tāreekh al-Islām more than other books, and it taught me how oblivious I am to how the Salaf actually thought, and how far we are from that.

My research led me to the scholars of Yemen from Ahlu as-Sunnah, whose methodology I found to be consistent with what I had already learned and trusted. I consult them (not as much as I would like, due to the distance), benefit from their fatwās. Shaykh Abū al-Yamān ʿAdnān al-Maṣqarī — may Allah preserve him — has written a preface for one of my works, which stands as a testimony to the approach I follow.

I am largely self-taught, and I say this openly. What matters is not the form of one's learning, but its soundness — verified always against the Book, the Sunnah, and the understanding of the Salaf.

Anyone who does not feel comfortable taking knowledge from me is free not to. That is their right, and I respect it.

May Allah make our knowledge sincere and beneficial.

entry.title: The Truth
entry.content:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم،

Allāh made this universe, and He, ʿazza wa jall, made our brains.

Our brains are programmable, meaning, what you feed them, what you repeat, what you train them to seek…becomes how they function.

So it follows that the best programming for the human mind is what Allāh commanded.

Because the One who made the mind is the One who gave the instructions.

The more a person aligns themselves with that guidance, the more correctly the mind operates: Clearer priorities, less confusion, less chasing illusions.

The mind starts functioning the way it was meant to!

Intelligence is not about appearing smart, or sounding modern, or saying smart things things, because that's just theater.

Being smart serves no better purpose than seeking the truth, and seeking the truth is what actually makes you smarter.

Why?
Because truth disciplines the mind.

It forces honesty, humility; it forces you to drop nonsense even when your ego likes it!

Falsehood does the opposite: it trains the brain to defend nonsense, justify contradictions, and that makes the cables tangled and messy.

It's that simple.

The more a person sincerely seeks the truth, the more their mind sharpens.

Not everyone becomes a genius, but everyone moves closer to the best version of the intellect Allāh gave them.

Truth improves the mind!

An improved mind recognizes truth more easily.

Rinse, and repeat.

"But...akhi...life is not that simple..."

I know I know...that's another story, called:

The heart.

entry.title: Dear Rose: Do Not Let Him Pick You
entry.content:
At first, it feels clean.

Actually, cleaner than I expected.

I always thought these things would be obvious.

A man who is not serious would sound unserious.

A man who wants to play would speak like someone playing.

But he is not like that.

He is careful with his words.

He does not say filthy things.

He does not push.

He does not make me feel cheap.

He asks about marriage.

He mentions my walī.

He says he wants things done properly.

That matters.

A careless man would not say that.

A man playing games would not speak about responsibility.

So when he asks how I am, I answer.

Why would I not?

It is just a question.

When he remembers something I said, I notice.

Of course I notice.

People do not usually pay attention like that.

When he says he was thinking about what I mentioned yesterday, something in me softens.

Not in a shameful way.

Just… in a human way.

It is nice to be heard.

It is nice to be spoken to gently.

It is nice when someone sees something in you and does not treat it carelessly.

And I am not foolish.

I know the limits.

I know where the line is.

We are not doing what other people do.

There is no flirting like that.

No vulgar speech.

No secret promises.

No nonsense.

Only careful words.

Only small messages.

Only enough to understand each other.

How else is a person supposed to know?

People say everything must go through the walī, and yes, of course.

But surely there has to be some understanding first.

Surely a man does not go to a family knowing nothing.

Surely a woman is allowed to know whether someone is serious.

And he does seem serious.

He says soon.

He says he is arranging things.

He says he wants the proper way.

Maybe he is just waiting for the right moment.

Maybe his situation is not easy.

Maybe I should be patient.

I would not want to be unfair.

And anyway, nothing has happened.

I am still myself.

I still pray.

I still know right from wrong.

I still have control over my heart.

I am not like the girls who get carried away.

I can stop if I need to.

I can keep things balanced.

It is only that my day feels a little different now.

When he writes, I feel lighter.

When he delays, I wonder why.

When something happens, I think of telling him.

When I read something beautiful, I wonder what he would say.

But that is normal, is it not?

When someone might become part of your life, of course you begin to make space for him in your thoughts.

That is not wrong by itself.

That is just how the heart prepares.

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

 

And perhaps this is how it starts for everyone.

A little attention.

A little hope.

A little fear.

A little waiting.

A flower does not know the moment it begins to lean toward the hand.

It only knows that the hand is warm.

That it returns.

That it does not crush.

That it seems to admire without taking.

So it remains still.

And when the fingers touch the petals, it does not pull away.

Why would it?

The touch is gentle.

The voice is gentle.

The intention seems gentle.

And the garden is still around it.

Nothing has been picked.

Not yet.

But then the hand returns again.

And again.

At first, that feels like seriousness.

A man who keeps returning must mean what he says.

A man who remembers must care.

A man who asks must be thinking ahead.

So I make room for him.

Not too much.

Only enough to be fair.

Only enough to understand.

Only enough to see where this might go.

Then my phone becomes part of the waiting.

Not always.

Not in a desperate way.

But I notice.

I notice when he writes earlier than usual.

I notice when he writes later.

I notice when his tone changes.

I notice when he says less.

I notice when he says more.

And I tell myself this is normal.

How can something serious move forward without some concern?

How can two people consider marriage while feeling nothing?

I am not attached.

I am only paying attention.

There is a difference.

But the difference becomes harder to explain.

When he is warm, I feel settled.

When he is distant, I feel restless.

When he mentions speaking properly, I feel relieved.

When another week passes, I tell myself there must be a reason.

And there is always a reason.

His family.

His work.

His money.

His uncertainty.

The timing.

The need to prepare.

The need to avoid rushing.

The need to make sure.

All of it sounds responsible.

All of it sounds careful.

And because I do not want to be immature, I accept the waiting.

I would hate to be one of those girls who pressures a man.

I would hate to ruin something good by being impatient.

So I become patient.

But my patience is no longer empty.

It has his name inside it.

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

 

I do not tell anyone.

Not because I am hiding something.

There is nothing to hide.

It is only too early.

Too unfinished.

Too delicate.

People misunderstand matters when they see them before they are complete.

If I mention him now, they will ask questions I cannot answer yet.

Has he spoken to your walī?

When will he come?

Who is his family?

What exactly does he want?

And I do not want to turn something still forming into a public matter.

So I keep it quiet.

For now.

Until there is something real to say.

And anyway, he does mention the proper way.

He does not deny it.

He does not mock it.

He does not say my walī does not matter.

He only says:

Soon.

When things are clearer.

When the moment is right.

And I believe him.

Or maybe I believe the version of him that has been living in my mind.

It is difficult to tell when hope starts completing a person’s sentences for him.

 

 

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

 

The flower is still in the garden.

That is what makes it easy to remain calm.

The stem has not been cut.

The roots have not been pulled out.

No one has carried it away.

But the soil around it has loosened.

Quietly.

Each visit moves something.

Each touch takes a little firmness from the ground.

Each delay teaches the flower to wait upward, toward the hand, instead of downward, into the root.

And because the petals are still bright, nobody notices.

Even the flower does not notice.

It thinks:

I am still here.

I am still safe.

I am still myself.

But its life has begun to gather around something outside the soil.

 

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

################################

 

 

Then one day, the hand does not return the same way.

Not cruelly.

That would almost be easier.

Cruelty gives the heart something clear to reject.

But this is softer.

A shorter reply.

A delayed answer.

A new difficulty.

A sentence that begins with:

I have been thinking.

Or:

My situation has changed.

Or:

I do not want to hurt you.

And suddenly all the waiting gathers in one place.

All the small excuses.

All the defended silences.

All the times I told myself soon.

All the ways I made room for him before he made a home for me.

The garden is still there.

My family is still there.

My walī is still there.

The proper door was always there.

But my heart had already been standing at another entrance.

A private one.

A quiet one.

One nobody forced open.

One I kept unlocked because I thought he was different.

And now I understand something I did not want to understand.

A flower does not have to be fully picked in one motion.

It can be loosened first.

Visited first.

Admired first.

Bent toward the hand first.

Made to live upward first.

Then, when it is finally taken, it almost feels natural.

And when it is left, it does not know how to stand as before.

entry.title: Step By Step, And You'll Grow So Big
entry.content:
Remember, do not think about tasks whole—your brain will choke.

"You mad?!", said the brain.
"Release depression and failure hormones!!!", the brain as well.

Divide a single task into sub-tasks.

فرق، تسود

Farriq, tasood.
Divide them, and you'll conquer them.

"Ohh....that's more like it!", says the brain.
"Ok ok ok, kill the depression switch, this human is back into his mind, being reasonable and all", the brain as well.

Humans love jumping to conclusions, it's easier, requires less effort, less scary.

1+1=11

Why do maths if you can stick them together?

That's what happens when you don't think through decisions and conclusions.

One decision like that after another, they snowball, and now you think you're a failure who's behind everyone and can't seem to be motivated to do anything. It always ends up locked...

Slow down, step by step, and you'll get there.

In Algeria, we tell toddlers who try to walk:

"داداش، تكبر قداش"

"Dāddāsh, tekber qaddāsh"
It's baby talk, not really Arabic.
Meaning, step by step, and you'll grow so big.

Imagine that toddler thinking about racing in the Olympics or whatever.

I can imagine the life draining out of their eyes. Such a huge gap.

But even the fastest runner was a toddler once.

entry.title: Have The Courage to Critique Frankly And Honestly
entry.content:
Cowards & Gossip. 

Why is it a common theme nowadays that Muslims are cowards? Why is it that those that have the most to say are those that do the least? 

Since I’ve arrived in Yemen I’ve consistently heard of people talking bad about me and others — specifically people I know who strive to do good. For some reason their tongue can only move in their absence. Is this sincerity? 

If someone has issues with what you do but they don’t “advise” you to your face it shows their lack of sincerity. As the Salaf mentioned, the real advisor is the one who advises you to your face, as for doing it in front of others — this is humiliation not advice! Then how about in their absence?!

If you have this characteristic you should be embarrassed. 

May Allāh protect us from people who listen to gossip and protect us from the gossipers. 

https://t.me/markazabuhurayrah

 

Strong tone, and sharp. Very necessary.

This phenomenon is also related to frankness, which I shared a clip of ibn Uthaymeen about it.

Also advice being a requirement between brothers in Eemaan.

And as mentioned by that post, courage is a necessity, because you can't confront someone who challenges your views without it. Especially if that someone has packed arguments that require a back and forth.

The best option here is to remain silent. However, one often doesn't, and instead releases that urge to speak and defend his views in a malicious way. 

I wrote something related to this, which you can find here:

https://en-armalqaddaaree.blogspot.com/2025/10/vague-critiques-hollow-guidance-fake.html?m=1

entry.title: Raising Thinkers, Not Repeaters
entry.content:
If you want to teach a child something, you must first understand it yourself. Not at the level of a scholar, but enough to give a mental model—a framework.

Don't dump details on children, plant seeds instead.

Children's minds are fertile soil. That's why they sometimes shock us with sharp observations. It's not magic. It's a fresh brain working from the roots up, without layers of bad assumptions.

When you notice that spark, stop and pay attention. That's a blessing. Grow it. Watch the questions they ask. Those questions are the mind revealing how it works and what it needs to reach its potential.

People are different, and children are people. Intelligence is not one thing.

When a child asks something you cannot answer, do not improvise nonsense. That kills curiosity, because the child senses that. It's like pouring water on a flame.

Say clearly: "I don't know. I'll ask someone knowledgeable". Or: "Let's do a research about it!", but only if you are qualified. Otherwise ask people who are.

That does something powerful. The spark stays alive. It intensifies. The child waits, thinks, anticipates. Sometimes they solve it themselves through logic. Sometimes they learn something deeper: this question matters. It’s big enough that even mommy or daddy must ask others.

Let them feel that. They need it.

That's how you grow a healthy plant. Later, it becomes a tree. Trees give fruit. Fruit carries seeds.

Do not limit the child. Teach them that knowledge is vast, and that scholars exist for a reason.

entry.title: Vague Critiques, Hollow Guidance, Fake Techniques, Blind Reliance
entry.content:
There’s a pattern I’ve noticed more than once, and it never fails to frustrate: someone throws a personal accusation your way, refuses to clarify, and leaves you in complete limbo. On the surface, it might seem like advice, a warning, or even concern—but dig a little deeper, and it’s a subtle power move.

The formula is simple: Accuse your opponent through a vague critique or claim. Refuse to clarify your claim if asked for specifics. Leave them confused, unsure how to respond, and questioning themselves.

What’s happening here isn’t accidental. The vagueness is deliberate: an attempt to assert authority without accountability, letting the other person weigh their critique over you while offering no way to engage meaningfully. The effect is immediate: frustration, withdrawal, and that sinking feeling that your effort, attempt to engage, understand, or connect, aren’t welcome.

This behavior has a name in psychology: gaslighting, and stonewalling. It’s manipulative, passive-aggressive, and exhausting. Yet it comes wrapped in a shiny wrapper of "guidance" or "concern", which makes it all the more frustrating.

This is no way to learn, and no way to build a relationship. Real growth, understanding, or collaboration cannot happen when one side holds all the cards and the other is left guessing. Genuine dialogue requires clarity, respect, and reciprocity—none of which exist in this pattern.

So yes, it’s frustrating. Yes, it kills your engagement. And maybe the only sane response is: step back and protect your energy from someone who’s more interested in asserting power than actually connecting, teaching, or creating something meaningful together.

entry.title: The Currency Of Sincerity — On the Decoupling of Expression and Reality
entry.content:
― ✦ ―

THE CURRENCY OF SINCERITY

— On the Decoupling of Expression and Reality —

AL-QADDĀRĪ

― ✦ ―

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيم

Introduction

Ash-shaykh Sulaymān al-Ruḥaylī noted that some people, whenever they meet someone, say "I love you for the sake of Allāh" — despite knowing of no reason that would warrant such love. He called this a mistake.

Indeed, it is a mistake.

Love for the sake of Allāh is not created by saying the words. The words are supposed to describe a reality that already exists — a reality rooted in the beloved's righteousness, his adherence to the Sunnah, his defense of the truth.

The love exists, it has real substance, and the statement merely informs the other person of that.

But if the cause disappears and the expression remains, the language drifts away from reality, which is the signature problem of our era's religious social culture.

― ✦ ―

The Inflation of
Religious Language

This dilution spreads across words, words that once carried immense gravity, words that suffered from over-circulation until their value faded away.

Praise is now effortless, and you can love immediately, and be a brother to anyone.

You can spend religious language freely, and not worry about the realities it was meant to represent.

Save the vocabulary only; the purchasing power is not our concern.

That leads to expressions being decoupled from their underlying substance, they cease to function as testimonies and begin to function more like decor.

This devastating effect is the consequence of a culture accustomed to immediate results, where individuals reach for the highest, most sacred language available to simulate an intimacy that has not yet been forged through trial or time.

They attempt to substitute the labor of building a true spiritual bond with the immediate gratification of declaring it.

The inevitable result of this over-printing is the opposite of the sought deep connection; a profound, unvoiced skepticism.

When the grandest terms are distributed indiscriminately, they lose their capacity to signify anything meaningful.

That in turn leads to hesitation to trust such language.

A logical response of a mind recognizing that the currency of speech has been thoroughly deflated.

― ✦ ―

The Precision Of the Salaf

These modern sensibilities run directly counter to the methodology of the salaf.

Let’s look at, for example, the encounter between Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī and Muʿāth bnu Jabal.

Abū Idrīs said to Muʿāth: "Wallāhi, I love you for the sake of Allāh".

Muʿāth did not return the words. Instead, he demanded: "Āllāh?"

An investigation.

Abū Idrīs answered: "Āllāh".

Muʿāth asked a second time: "Āllāh?"

Abū Idrīs repeated: "Āllāh".

Muʿāth asked a third time: "Āllāh?"

Abū Idrīs answered: "Āllāh".

Abū Idrīs offered no objection, no defensive pivot; he simply answered the great Companion with absolute submission to the gravity of the oath.

Only then did Muʿāth take hold of his garment, pull him close, and say: "Rejoice—for I heard the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ say: Allāh tabāraka wa taʿālā said: 'My love is due to those who love one another in Me, who sit together in Me, who visit one another in Me, and who give to one another in Me'".

Three times he asked. An interrogation.

Modern sensibilities detect this as emotional coldness.

But Muʿāth understood that "I love you for the sake of Allāh" is not a social greeting. It is a testimony. A testimony requires that the one giving it knows precisely what he is standing behind.

The testimony was given its right, and was not treated lightly.

The two men dealt with an immense reality. One carefully brought it forward; the other received it only after its weight was verified.

That’s the precision of the salaf. Their love had causes. Their praise had causes. Their criticism had causes.

Speech was not dictated by sentiment, but by an underlying reality they could stand behind.

We managed to reverse this successfully. We deploy the expression, then pretend its substance follows through automatically. Then, we act surprised when real circumstances expose this naivety.

The fragmentation of contemporary social ties ceases to be a mystery, then.

― ✦ ―

Verbal Softness

This reversal creates an obvious problem.

When language no longer guarantees reality, trust breaks down. Yet people still need a way to judge who is safe and who is virtuous.

They need a shortcut. People love shortcuts.

To fill that gap, we made a distorted version of adab and allowed it to settle into our consciousness. A version that reduces character entirely to a style of communication. The peel.

To many, good manners now mean soft speech, frequent affirmations, and pleasant phrasing. The warmer the voice, the more adab is assumed to be present.

But to the Salaf, adab was far deeper. It wasn't a style; it was truthfulness, fairness, accuracy, and placing matters exactly where they belong.

The softness of speech and the reality of adab are not the same thing. One does not guarantee the other.

A person can speak gently while being insincere.

A person can speak warmly while being manipulative.

A person can speak pleasantly while being unjust.

And a person can speak plainly while possessing excellent character.

The distortion of adab then leads to a distortion elsewhere:

When verbal warmth becomes the standard, two things happen:

An entire category of sincere people gets misread and wronged.

An entire category of insincere people gets passed off as virtuous.

Injustice wrapped in social niceties.

― ✦ ―

Temperament & Character

One reason this happens is because many people unconsciously treat their preferred temperament as the Islamic standard.

People who perform closeness easily have usually never had to question it. Nothing objected to it, so it settled into the shape of the truth.

So when they meet someone who does not operate that way, they do not think different. They think deficient. They do not observe — they diagnose.

The reserved individual becomes a case study. Something to be fixed.

Confusing concepts leads to a flawed perception of reality.

Because temperament describes how a person naturally expresses himself.

Character describes whether he is truthful, sincere, trustworthy, fair, loyal, and beneficial.

These categories overlap at times, but they are not identical.

A warm person can possess poor character.

A reserved person can possess excellent character.

An expressive person can be unreliable.

A quiet person can be deeply loyal.

The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ were not a single temperamental type.

ʿUmar bnu al-Khaṭṭāb was known for his directness, his sharpness, and his formidable presence.

Abū Bakr was quieter and softer.

ʿUthmān was famously shy.

Abū Tharr was frank in his disposition.

Each was distinct, and the Prophet ﷺ did not instruct any of them to converge on a single emotional style.

The Prophetic model does not demand temperamental uniformity. It demands character. It demands truthfulness, justice, loyalty, and the fulfillment of rights.

Human temperaments differ. Character standards do not.

― ✦ ―

Selective Expression

Once warmth is mistaken for the substance of adab, it follows naturally that visibility becomes the sole metric of character. If it is noticeable, you are mannered; if it dips, you lack manners.

To be considered virtuous within this framework, one must remain in a state of constant performance.

Let’s look at another example where the salaf demonstrated immense social intelligence, awareness, and real bonding.

ʿUmar bnu al-Khaṭṭāb once sought entry to see the Prophet ﷺ. He asked a servant to seek permission for him. The servant went in, spoke to the Prophet ﷺ, and returned to inform ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ had remained silent.

ʿUmar did not interpret this silence as an insult or a personal rejection; he simply withdrew and sat near the pulpit.

Driven by concern, he returned a second time, only for the exact same silence to occur. He sat down again. Only on his third attempt was he granted entry.

Upon entering, ʿUmar found the Prophet ﷺ lying on a bare reed mat that left deep impressions on his side, leaning against a leather pillow stuffed with harsh palm fiber.

ʿUmar greeted him and, while still standing, asked a direct question about whether he had divorced his wives. The Prophet ﷺ raised his eyes and answered with a single word: "No".

This exchange reveals something far deeper than a fatigued leader being brief. It demonstrates that the established reality of their bond was doing the heavy lifting, completely independent of verbal validation.

ʿUmar was turned away twice without receiving it as a slight or a sign of fractured brotherhood.

When he finally received that one-word answer, he did not treat the brevity as a deficiency or demand an artificial display of warmth from the Prophet ﷺ.

Instead, he read the state of the room, calibrated his approach with light conversation to ease the tension, and waited for the warmth to emerge naturally and unforced.

Prophetic adab, therefore, is not a generalized emotional warmth broadcast uniformly in all directions.

Selective, considered, and grounded expression is inherently closer to this standard than perpetual performative enthusiasm.

Consistency of performance is not the Islamic standard. Sincerity of reality is.

― ✦ ―

Distance, Closeness,
and the Salaf

Al-imām al-Khaṭṭābī, in his book al-ʿUzlah (Seclusion), preserves a series of accounts that reframe the entire modern assumption about what closeness between brothers should look like.

Shabīb bnu Shayba said: "Among my brothers are those who visit me only once a year — these are the ones I take and count upon in life and death. And among them are those who visit me every day, who kiss me and whom I kiss — and if I could replace my kiss with a bite, I would bite them".

A full year of physical absence, and yet they remained true brothers.

Daily meetings, but nothing concrete.

The frequency of contact was entirely decoupled from the actual weight of the bond.

ʿAbdu ar-Raḥmān bnu Mahdī and Yaḥyā bnu Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān were known for their deep bond. Yet a year would frequently pass without a single face-to-face meeting between them. When one was asked about this, he said: "When hearts are close, physical distance does no harm".

The poet says:

I saw two intimate friends parting in virtue
when hearts had settled upon sincere affection.
Only the one suspicious of his own love
keeps visiting constantly.

This rigorous standard runs consistently through the heritage of the early generations.

Bishr bnu al-Ḥārith said: "The most beloved of my brothers to me is the one who neither sees me nor do I see him".

And when Sufyān ath-Thawrī was asked to point out a man whose companionship was genuinely worth seeking, he replied with heavy realism: "That is something that cannot be found".

These are not the words of cold or indifferent men. These are the words of men who understood that the reality of brotherhood resides securely in the heart and manifests in concrete action when it truly matters—not in the superficial frequency of visits, modern check-ins, or verbal declarations.

The poet said:

My brother is not the one who befriends me with his tongue
but the one who stands with me in calamities.
Whose wealth is mine when I am destitute,
and mine is his when time presses hard upon him.
Do not praise a companion during ease
for brothers often turn away when disasters come.

― ✦ ―

Emotional Seriousness

The divergence in how people communicate is not merely a difference in style; it is a difference in how they view the weight of language itself.

Some speak freely because words come easily to them. Others speak cautiously because words carry the weight of a debt.

Praise is a testimony.

Love is a serious judgment.

Loyalty is a lifelong commitment.

Affection is a heavy responsibility.

Because these concepts carry such immense gravity, these individuals hesitate to spend large words on small realities.

They refuse to use the vocabulary of deep spiritual bonds to describe casual, unearned interactions. This scarcity of expression is never evidence of emotional poverty; it is the manifestation of emotional seriousness.

The friction arises because the highly expressive type rarely understands that this second way of being exists. Because their own emotional style feels natural and universally correct, they have quietly mistaken performative warmth for the baseline of human decency.

They do not realize that someone else might be experiencing a reality too deep to easily verbalize.

― ✦ ―

What Brotherhood Actually Requires

The word "brotherhood" is deployed constantly in contemporary spaces, completely detached from its weight.

What it has become, in reality, is a contract nobody signed: be present constantly, respond warmly, and perform closeness visibly enough that the other person feels reassured.

If that warmth ever dips, and even for reasons completely unrelated to the bond itself—something is automatically assumed to be wrong. With you.

True brotherhood requires no such maintenance. When the foundation is solid, distance is merely a circumstance—not a threat.

A real bond depends on what a person is actually made of, not on how well they perform when they are right in front of you.

A person can perform social warmth flawlessly, mastering the external posture of intimacy, while possessing absolutely no capacity for a deeper bond.

A person can be reserved, even terse, and remain entirely unshakeable when the weight of life demands a true ally.

The man who stands by you in hardship, who shields your honor in you absence, who tells you the uncomfortable truth when you need to hear it—this is a brother, irrespective of his verbal output.

Brotherhood is not a matter of shared emotional styles. It is what remains when the warmth of words is tested by the coldness of circumstance.

― ✦ ―

The penalty of prematurity

مَنْ تَعَجَّلَ شَيْئًا قَبْلَ أَوَانِهِ عُوقِبَ بِحِرْمَانِهِ.

Whoever rushes a thing before its proper time is punished by being deprived of it.

The jurists (al-fuqahāʾ) established this profound maxim regarding human actions and their consequences.

A principle which the modern demand for instant intimacy continually violates.

True connection, mutual trust, and spiritual love are fruits that grow on a specific, unalterable timeline. They require the slow accumulation of shared trials, proven consistency, and time.

When people attempt to bypass this process—using the heaviest, most sacred vocabulary of brotherhood to force an intimacy that has not yet been forged—they trigger the exact spiritual penalty described by the jurists.

By demanding the immediate rewards of deep companionship before its proper time, we are punished with its ultimate deprivation.

We receive the performative wrapper, but lose the substance.

We are left with an exhausting loop of mutual reassurance, always sensing underneath it that the foundation cannot bear the weight of the words.

Seen in this light, the reserved stance is not an emotional deficiency or a social awkwardness awaiting correction. It is a quiet, disciplined adherence to the law of timing.

The refusal to broadcast unearned warmth is an act of preservation. It recognizes that if a profound bond is ever to exist between two people, it cannot be conjured through premature declarations. It must be allowed its proper time, protected by a measured silence until the reality catches up to the language.

― ✦ ―

Conclusion

Words are not realities; they are merely signs pointing toward them.

The one who understands this, refuses to speak until the word is true, they reserve expression for what has been earned, and allow silence to carry what speech cannot.

They honor the true weight of a testimony.

But, modern sensibilities look at these people and diagnose them as cold, which says everything about the superficiality of contemporary social culture, and nothing about their character.

This goes far deeper than a few cheapened phrases. We have built a culture where knowing the vocabulary is routinely mistaken for mastering the framework.

And, in a time when language has never been cheaper, those who guard their words are not a problem to be corrected.

They are a rare and necessary reminder of what sincerity actually looks like.

We are the problem, as we failed to recognize them.

هذا، والله أعلم.
وصلى الله على نبينا محمد.

entry.title: التربية
Will I Ever Get Married?
entry.content:
Ash-shaykh ʿAmmār al-Ḥawbānī:

The Prophet ﷺ said: "O young people, whoever among you is able to marry should marry, and whoever cannot should fast, for it is a restraint for him".

Do not preoccupy yourself with what you do not currently possess. If you are not yet married and you do not have the means or ability, do not burden your heart with it. Do not let it consume your attention.

Seek knowledge, and goodness will certainly come to you, by the permission of Allāh.

How many people sought knowledge while not owning a single coin, yet Allāh opened doors for them through knowledge itself. People began competing for them, even rushing to arrange marriage for them, as was seen in Dammaj.

And how many at the beginning of their path desired marriage, but when they were unable, they turned fully to seeking knowledge. They had no wealth, and not even the knowledge that would make others aspire to them.

Then, after learning and understanding the religion, they became prominent figures. People competed to marry them, while they themselves sometimes declined. Their hearts became more composed, more restrained, less distracted by women and worldly attachments. Then later, they married.

The key point is this: seek knowledge, and goodness will come.

Do not set in your heart a hidden intention like: I will seek knowledge so that I can get married through it. That is a bad intention.

But if Allāh knows good in your hearts, He will grant you good.

Do not overthink worldly matters.

In the narration of Zayd bnu Thābit: "…and whoever makes the Hereafter his main concern, Allāh gathers his affairs, places sufficiency in his heart, and the worldly life comes to him willingly".

Many people never expected marriage before seeking knowledge. They used to think: I will travel, stay away for years, save money, then return, build a house, then start searching for a spouse.

This is the reality for many: years of travel and hardship, followed by growing financial pressure around marriage, leading to frustration.

Then some of them turn to seeking knowledge, and within a short time Allāh opens doors for them. Good comes to them, they marry, their life stabilizes, their provision continues, and they remain in seeking knowledge, eating and living modestly while preserving themselves.

That is the true provision.

How many people have chosen for themselves the path of seeking knowledge, while others chose expatriation and years away from home in order to accumulate wealth? Yet the one who sought knowledge ends up marrying, Allāh opens doors for him, and he is blessed with children, while the other remains abroad to this day.

I know many stories of this kind, which shows that this path is indeed a path of goodness.

However, if a person is unable to marry, then he should be patient and not allow it to occupy his heart, especially at the beginning of his studies. He should supplicate to Allāh, devote himself to what is before him, and goodness will come to him, by the permission of Allāh, the Most High.

We have mentioned this because these are important matters that need to be brought to the attention of young men, and young women as well. A beginner student of knowledge, whether male or female, should direct his or her energies toward seeking knowledge. That is the aspiration that ought to occupy them.

As for marriage and the affairs of this worldly life, they will come as a consequence and inevitably in due course.

The more a person increases in knowledge, the more Allāh surrounds him with His care, honors him from His vast bounty, and grants him from His gifts.

He is a slave of Allāh. Would Allāh abandon him, while granting provision to disbelievers, polytheists, and sinners who neither return to Him nor repent to Him? What a wretched way of thinking that is.


Original transcript:

قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:
"يا معشر الشباب، من استطاع منكم الباءة فليتزوج، ومن لم يستطع فعليه بالصوم، فإنه له وجاء".

ولا تشغل نفسك بما لا تملكه: إن لم تكن قد تزوجت، ولا عندك قدرة ولا استطاعة، فلا تُتعب قلبك بذلك. لا تُشغل نفسك.
اطلب العلم، وسيأتيك الخير يقينًا بإذن الله.

فكم من إنسان طلب العلم، ولم يكن يملك درهمًا واحدًا، ففتح الله عليه بالعلم، فتنافس الناس عليه، وتزاحموا في تزويجه، كما رأينا في دماج.
وكم من إنسان في بداية طلبه كان يتطلع إلى الزواج، فلما عجز أقبل على طلب العلم، ولم يكن عنده مال، ولا حتى علم يُطمع به الناس.
فلما طلب العلم وتفقه في الدين، صار ممن يُشار إليهم بالبنان، وتنافس الناس على تزويجه، وهو يرفض أحيانًا، وقد صار في زهد وتأني، لا يلتفت إلى النساء وما إلى ذلك، ثم تزوج بعد ذلك.

والشاهد: اطلب العلم يأتيك الخير.
ولا تجعل في قرارة نفسك: إني سأطلب العلم، وأجتهد لأجل أن يُزوجوني. فهذه نية سيئة.
لكن إن يعلم الله في قلوبكم خيرًا يؤتكم خيرًا.

فلا تُفكر كثيرًا في الدنيا. وفي حديث زيد بن ثابت: "ومن كانت الآخرة همه، جمع الله عليه شمله، وجعل غناه في قلبه، وأتته الدنيا وهي راغمة".

وكثير من الناس ما كان يتوقع أنه سيتزوج قبل طلب العلم. كان يقول: سأغترب، كم سأبقى؟ أحتاج سنوات أجمع فيها المال، ثم أعود لأبني بيتًا، ثم أبحث عن الزواج.
وهذا واقع كثير من الناس: يغترب سنين طويلة، ثم تتراكم عليه تكاليف الزواج فيصاب بالإحباط.

ثم إذا أقبل بعضهم على طلب العلم، ما هي إلا أيام حتى يفتح الله عليه، ويسوق له الخير، فيتزوج، وتنتظم حياته، ويأتيه رزقه، ويستمر في طلب العلم، يأكل ويشرب ويعف نفسه مع الاستمرار.

وهكذا الرزق الحقيقي.

كم من إنسان ارتضى لنفسه طلب العلم، وآخر ارتضى لنفسه الغربة لجمع المال، فذاك قد يتزوج الذي طلب العلم وفتح الله عليه، ورُزق ذرية، بينما الآخر لا يزال في الغربة.
وأعرف قصصًا كثيرة في هذا الباب، مما يدل على أنه باب خير.

لكن إن لم يستطع الإنسان فليصبر نفسه، ولا يُشغل قلبه، خاصة في بداية الطلب. يدعو الله، ويقبل على شأنه، وسيأتيه الخير بإذن الله سبحانه وتعالى.

وإنما ذكرنا ذلك لأن هذه المعاني مهمة أن تُنبه للشباب، بل وللشابات أيضًا. فينبغي لطالب العلم المبتدئ، وطالبة العلم المبتدئة، أن يُقبلوا على العلم، فهذه هي الهمة المطلوبة.

وأما الزواج وأمور الدنيا فهي ستأتي تبعًا ولا محالة.
فكلما ازداد الإنسان علمًا، كلما أحاطه الله برعايته، وأكرمه من واسع فضله، وأمده من عطاياه.

فهو عبد لله، أيتركه، ثم يعطي الكفار والمشركون والعصاة الذين لا يرجعون إليه ولا يتوبون له؟ بئس هذا التفكير. 

https://t.me/mnamk/6553

entry.title: Hold On...Your Lord Is Generous
entry.content:
مهلًا، فربك كريم

Hold on — your Lord is Generous.

قال الله تعالى: {قُلْ عَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ قَرِيبًا} [الإسراء: 51].

Allaah, Exalted is He, said: { Say: Perhaps it will be soon } [Al-Israa': 51]

في هذه الآية تسلية للمؤمن المنتظر وفرج للأمل الكامن في صدره،

This verse is soothing for believers who wait, and a relief for the hope hidden within their chests.

فهي تذكره أن وعد الله لا يطول على من صدق،

It reminds them that the promise of Allaah is never far for those who truly believe.

وأن ما يتمناه من خير قد يكون أقرب مما يظن،

And that the good they long for may be nearer than they imagine.

ولكن الحكيم سبحانه يؤخر لحكمة

Yet the All-Wise, Holy is He, delays for a reason full of wisdom,

ويعطي في الوقت الأنسب لعبده،

and grants at the most suitable time for His slaves.

فلتبقى القلوب معلقة بربها

So let hearts remain attached to their Lord,

واثقة أن التأخير ليس نسيانًا بل إعدادًا،

trusting that delay is not neglect, but preparation.

وأن ما كتب الله كائن في أوانه،

And that what Allaah has decreed will occur in its appointed time.

فلا تيأس إذا أبطأت الأمنية،

So do not despair when your wish seems slow to come.

فربك يقول: قل عسى أن يكون قريبًا،

For your Lord has said: Say, perhaps it will be soon.

فكن على يقين أنه قريب حقًا وإن لم تره بعد.

So be certain that it truly is near, even if you have not seen it yet.

أبو المنذر الحوباني

Abu l-Munthir al-Hawbaanee.

entry.title: The Compendium of The Correct Creed - Lesson 1
entry.content:
Description:

1. Important introduction on the importance of seeking knowledge
2. What is the greatest hadeeth clarifying the levels of the religion?
3. List the narrations of this hadeeth and the Companions who narrated it.
 

Transcription:

All praise is due to Allah.
and I bear witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, alone without partner.
And I bear witness that Muhammad is His slave and messenger. May Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, his family, and his companions abundantly.
To proceed:
My brothers in Allah, I want to remind myself and you, that a Muslim must make use of his lifetime, which Allah, Exalted He is, has granted him.
We must make use of this life, and the hours that remain from our lives.
Allah, Exalted He is, said:
O you who believe, fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has sent forth for tomorrow.
يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَلْتَنْظُرْ نَفْسٌ مَا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ
So whoever Allah has gifted blessings, must recognize Allah’s blessings upon him.
The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, as in Saheeh al-Bukhaaree from Ibn Abbaas, may Allah be pleased with them both:
Two blessings many people lose out on: health and free time.
نعمتان مغبون فيهما كثير من الناس: الصحة والفراغ.

So whoever Allah has granted health and well-being, and has free time must use this life, and this free time in obeying Allah, Exalted He is.
Using life well is by doing righteous deeds, and these righteous deeds, along with faith, are the path to a good life.
So whoever wants to live a good life, a life with no misery, a life with no fear or grief, whoever wants the path to a good life, then it comes from faith and righteous deeds.
What is the proof for this?
Allah, Exalted He is, said:
Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely give him a good life.
من عمل صالحا من ذكر أو أنثى وهو مؤمن فلنحيينه حياة طيبة

This is a promise from Allah, and Allah does not break His promise.
So we must learn faith, and know what the righteous deeds are, so that we live a good life in this world, and live a good life in the Hereafter.
Faith and righteous deeds cannot be known, except through knowledge.
We must have beneficial knowledge, O brothers, we must learn this faith, and learn righteous deeds.
Because seeking knowledge is an obligation, just as prayer is an obligation, zakah is an obligation, fasting is an obligation.
Seeking knowledge too is an obligation.
This came from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as in the hadeeth of Anas, and other companions, from several companions:
the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
طلب العلم فريضة على كل مسلم
Narrated by ibn Maajah and al-Bayhaqee.
Al-Haafith ibn Abd al-Barr gathered its chains in his book *Jami' Bayaan al-Ilm wa Fadhlih*, and said the hadeeth is sound, and is authentic.
Shaykh al-Albaany also authenticated it in *Saheeh at-Targheeb*.
So this is a great hadeeth showing us that seeking knowledge is an obligation.
We must strive, you and us together, in seeking knowledge.
May Allah bless you.
Allah, Exalted He is, raises you through this knowledge,
as He said:
Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees.
كما قال الله يرفع الله الذين آمنوا منكم والذين أوتوا العلم درجات

And the angels do not lower their wings for a president nor a minister;
they only lower them for the seeker of knowledge.
As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
The angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge, pleased with what he seeks.
الملائكة تضع أجنحتها لطالب العلم رضا بما يطلب

So feel this, O seeker of knowledge:
when you seek knowledge, even by listening to these lessons, you are considered a seeker of knowledge.
The angels lower their wings for you.
You are considered among the best of people, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
The best of you are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it.
خيركم من تعلم القرآن وعلمه

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him:
For one of you to go to the mosque and learn two verses, is better for him than two she-camels; three is better than three; four is better than four..and so on.
لأن يغدو أحدكم إلى المسجد فيتعلم آيتين خير له من ناقتين وثلاث خير له من ثلاث، وأربع خير له من أربع، وبأعدادهن

And the proofs of the virtue of knowledge are many.
May Allah reward you with goodness.
So, we want to make every day a short lesson in the matters of creed that concern Muslims and that Muslims must learn.
If Allah wills, we will start from today with this light lesson.
Whoever wants to write it in a notebook, take these benefits and review them—in time, if Allah wills, they will gain much good, by Allah’s permission.
The main thing is not to get bored—one must not get bored of knowledge, nor be distracted from it by worldly matters.
So let’s begin directly, if Allah wills, and we will make it in the form of points, so it is easier for the listener.
We said we must learn the religion, learn the religion of Islam.
So, the first question, the first point, is:
What is the greatest hadeeth in this topic—the levels of religion and learning them?
Which is the greatest hadeeth regarding this?
and the answer to that is: That the greatest hadeeth in this topic, the topic of the levels of religion, is a hadeeth called: the long hadeeth of Jibreel.
The long hadeeth of Jibreel.
Most of you probably know this hadeeth:
the hadeeth of Umar ibn al-Khattaab, may Allah be pleased with him.
He said:
While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, one day, there appeared before us a man with extremely white clothes, extremely black hair.
No sign of travel was seen on him, and none of us knew him.
He came and sat before the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and put his knees against his knees, and placed his hands on his thighs
meaning, he sat as a knowledge seeker, on his knees, his palms on his thighs, facing the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him,
and said: O Muhammad!
and the companions are listening, and they don't know this man.
He said: "O Muhammad, tell me about Islam".
So this is the first thing, tell me about Islam.
So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
"Islam is to bear witness that there is no deity except Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,
to establish prayer,
to give zakah,
to fast Ramadhaan,
and to perform pilgrimage to the House if you are able to".
He said, "You have spoken the truth."
So we were amazed—he asks him, then says, "You have spoken the truth,"

How does one ask another, then says: "You have spoken the truth"? Meaning he already knows the answer.
Then he said, "And tell me about faith".
He said: "Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. And to believe in the Devine Decree, its good and its bad".
He said, "You have spoken the truth".
Then he said, "And tell me about excellence"
He said: "Excellence is to worship Allah as though you see Him; if you do not see Him, He sees you".
He said, "Tell me about the Hour".
He said: "The one asked knows no more than the questioner".
He said, "Tell me about its signs".
He said: "That a slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in building tall buildings".
He said: He then he left, and I [Umar] waited a while, then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:
"O Umar, do you know who the questioner was?"
I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best."
He said: "It was Jibreel; he came to teach you your religion".
Look! He said "your religion".
So *this* is religion, it is these levels: Islaam, Eemaan (faith), and Ihsaan (excellence).
So this hadeeth, this great hadeeth, called the long hadeeth of Jibreel, is the greatest hadeeth regarding the levels of religion, because it clarifies them: Islam, then Eemaan (faith), then Ihsaan (excellence).
And if Allah wills, we will later explain these matters in detail.
But this lesson’s point is: who narrated this hadeeth?
Because one must know who narrated a hadeeth and its authenticity—it’s not for anyone to just say, "The Messenger of Allah said…", you have to know who narrated it and its status.
So: This hadeeth was narrated by several companions. First, by Umar ibn al-Khattaab in Saheeh Muslim; also by Abu Hurayrah in al-Bukhaaree and Muslim; and by five other companions mentioned by Ibn Hajar in *Fath al-Baaree*:
Abu Tharr, Ibn Umar, Anas, Jareer ibn Abdullaah, Ibn Abbaas, and Abu Aamir al-Ashari—and this is outside the two Saheehs. The hadeeth is authentic and is a great hadeeth.
Imam Muslim began his Saheeh with this hadeeth.
As for al-Bukhaaree, the first hadeeth in his Saheeh is the hadeeth of Umar:
Actions are only by intentions.
إنما الأعمال بالنيات
Imam an-Nawawee, in his *Forty hadeeths*, began with *Actions are only by intentions*, and then made the second hadeeth the long hadeeth of Jibreel.
Al-Baghawi did the same in *Misabaah as-Sunnah*. He made this hadeeth, the hadeeth of Umar bnu al-Khattaab: *Actions are only by intentions* the first, then the second, the long hadeeth of Jibreel.
So we know this hadeeth is a great hadeeth.
This is today’s benefit: the greatest hadeeth on the pillars of Islam, Eemaan (faith), and Ihsaan (excellence) is the long hadeeth of Jibreel, narrated by Muslim from Umar, and by al-Bukhaaree and Muslim from Abu Hurayrah.
This is today’s benefit and today’s lesson.
We ask Allah, Exalted He is, to benefit us and you with what we have heard.
We ask Allah, Exalted He is, to grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.
And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Published on: 

4th of Rabee' al-Awwal 1447 AH

entry.title: Al-Albaany’s Diagnosis Of The Disease That Is Ravaging The Da'wah to Islaam today
entry.content:
تشخيص الألباني للمرض الذي يفتك بالدعوة إلى الإسلام اليوم

الشيخ: كنت أظنُّ أن المشكلة في العالم الإسلامي إنما هي فقط ابتعادهم عن فهمهم لحقيقة معنى لا إله إلا الله ، ولكني مع الزمن صرتُ أتبيَّن أن هناك مشكلة أخرى في هذا العالم تُضاف إلى المشكلة الأولى الأساسية ؛ ألا وهي بعدهم عن التوحيد ، المشكلة الأخرى أنهم أكثرهم لا يتخلَّقون بأخلاق الإسلام الصحيحة إلا بقدرٍ زهيدٍ.

Al-Albaany’s Diagnosis Of The Disease That Is Ravaging The Da'wah to Islaam today

The shaykh: I used to think that the problem in the Islamic world was only being far from understanding the true meaning of laa ilaaha illa Allaah. But with time I came to realize that there is another problem in this world in addition to that primary one: them being far from tawheed. The other problem is that most of them do not embody the correct manners of Islaam except to a very small degree.

Source: https://www.al-albany.com/audios/content/142714/
 
I said: Among the reasons this sickness has grown more severe: social media.
The worst of them are Facebook and similar, and the least harmful are Telegram and WhatsApp.

Whether people like that or not.

We insist that whoever advises the youth to use them under the pretext of "competing with the disbelievers" has made a mistake. 

That is because most young people are overtaken by zeal and impulsiveness, so they publish everything they come across.

Dry grass and a spark of fire.

What should we expect from that? Nothing but chaos and tribulations.

Just as it is not suitable for everyone to author books, the same applies to posting, because it requires knowledge, wisdom, and deliberation.
At the very least, those who post online should consult someone whose knowledge they trust about what they intend to publish, just as a beginning author consults someone trustworthy in knowledge about what they have authored.

I say this as advice to myself and to my brothers. Do not find the truth burdensome, and do not be deceived by what you have become accustomed to.

entry.title: Text, Tone, and Misreadings
entry.content:
Text flattens people.

It carries ideas, but it does not carry voice, pauses, or facial cues. What would sound calm and welcoming in speech can appear sharp once written, even when the intent is unchanged.

This is clearer in technical discussions. Clear conclusions and direct reasoning often read louder between letters than they do in real conversation.

Certainty, in text, is easily mistaken for harshness, arrogance, being a "know-it-all". That is not always a matter of character; often it is a property of the medium itself.

People also differ in how they communicate. Some prefer a gradual, softened approach. Others state the conclusion plainly and then walk through the reasoning. These are methods, and they reflect style, not the state of a person's heart.

It helps to keep things from getting mixed, to realize that:
* An argument is weighed by its evidence.
* Tone shapes how that argument is received in a given context.
* Intentions, however, are not visible to others. Those belong to a different domain altogether, and they are known only to Allāh.

So when something written feels firm, understand that firmness is directed at ideas, not at people. And when words come across sharper than intended, that is often a limitation of text, not a reflection of character.

Allāh knows best.

entry.title: Conversational Narcissism
entry.content:
I learned something new, which helped me pin-point what exactly bothered me about some people, both in real life and online. So I thought it might help you as well and give your mind some rest and ease, inshāʾa Allāh.


Apparently, there is something called "conversational narcissism". It's when a person dominates conversations and consistently redirects the focus onto themselves.

They often speak in long monologues, show little genuine interest in others, and even when they seem attentive, it's usually just to find an opening to insert themselves back into the conversation.

The most obvious sign is that they seem oblivious, they ramble excessively, sometimes at inappropriate moments, talking mostly about themselves, their desires, or plans. This leads to a disconnect: between the conversation participants and between the discussion and its original topic.

Why do they behave this way? There are many reasons. It's not always malicious; sometimes they’re simply unaware of how they come across.

The effect on others, however, is consistent: alienation, disinterest, feeling overwhelmed, and often a sense of bizarreness.

If you need to interact with such a person, the best approach is to be gentle but honest. Let them know how you feel, using plenty of "I" statements like "I feel…" to make them aware of your perspective, and that you're a human being with feelings, not an audience behind a screen.
If that doesn't work, then you need more directness, and use methods like redirecting with questions, pausing, or calmly pointing out the topic drift. Polite frankness helps a lot here.

Allāh knows best.

entry.title: Ask the People Who Understand The Tools
entry.content:
Ask tech-savvy people, and do that early, not casually or as an afterthought. Early.

People who live around tools start seeing things others don't even realize exist. Little cracks, hidden hinges, quiet risks sitting behind ordinary buttons.

Most people think using a tool equals understanding it, but that’s rarely true.

You can post, upload, share links, create channels, grow followers, and still not understand the structure underneath any of it.

We know that the internet is structure, layers upon layers, systems talking to systems, permissions, identities, recovery methods, hidden doors you don't see until someone else walks through them first.

The internet requires expertise.

Not genius, or elite knowledge, just people who actually know what they're doing.

That kind of person is called: A specialist.
Not a guesser, and definitely not an improviser.

Before Competing, Understand the Tools

Many people speak about competing with falsehood online, spreading benefit, countering harm, being present where others are present.

That part makes sense.

But there is a skipped step.

Understanding the battlefield.

Because when people don't understand the tools they're using, they don't really control their efforts. They borrow systems without understanding their limits.

And when something goes wrong, they don't know how to respond properly, because they were never trained for it.

Good Intentions Need Technical Support

A person can be sincere, dedicated, motivated to benefit others.

But sincerity does not automatically produce technical awareness.

Just like someone can want to drive safely but still not understand how brakes fail, how tires wear down, how engines overheat.

You don't learn those things by intention.

You learn them from people who already know.

You need someone who has handled the tool long enough to know its moods.

Every field has them.

Photography has them.
Software has them.
Platforms have them.
Security has them.

And ignoring them doesn't make the risk disappear. It only makes the surprise bigger when something eventually breaks.

We Already Accept This in Other Fields

Think about photography.

I keep telling people: ask experts about photography before forming strong conclusions. Not because photography is mysterious, but because the technical side of it is deeper than it looks.

The same applies to platforms.

The same applies to the internet.

We shouldn't assume that because something looks simple on the surface, it is simple underneath.

Most of the time, simplicity is an interface — not a reality.

Behind every clean button sits a complicated mechanism. 

The Internet Rewards Preparedness

The internet moves fast.

Mistakes spread faster than corrections. Confusion spreads faster than clarity. Problems multiply quietly before they become visible.

And once something goes wrong, it often affects more than the person running the platform.

It affects everyone connected to them: followers, readers, students, listeners.

That is why relying on expertise is a responsibility.

Not panic or suspicion, just responsibility. Careful and slow and steady.

Ask Before You Build

Before launching platforms.
Before building audiences.
Before depending on systems.

Ask the people who understand the tools.

And not just once, no: Repeatedly.

Let them point out risks you didn't see. Weaknesses you didn't imagine. Simple protections that cost little but prevent massive problems later.

Because the internet is not forgiving to assumption.

But it is surprisingly kind to preparation.

And many problems that look sudden… were preventable long before they happened.

If someone had just asked:

"Who here actually understands how this works?".

Finally, please don't assume these experts will know everything either, don't jump from one end to the other. They are humans who make mistakes too.

The Prophet ṣallā-Allāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam said:

Whoever undertakes medical treatment among people without being known for medical practice beforehand, and he causes harm, is held responsible (liable for the damage).
Source: Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4587.
Classed as ḥasan (sound) by al-Albānī in Ṣaḥīḥ Abī Dāwūd.

The point of evidence here is what we derive through mafhūm al-mukhālafah (argument by contrast), meaning that anyone who is known to possess the skill (profession) bears no liability.

هذا والله أعلم.

entry.title: Translate "عبد" as "Slave"
entry.content:
Not "servant", and not "worshipper". None of that.

It is: slave.

"But that's degrading!".

So it was in al-Jāhiliyyah. Then Islām came and taught them that being a slave of Allāh is a high rank.

English does not naturally carry this concept.

Christians are the ones who use "servant", which is wrong. Very wrong.

We do not serve Allāh.

We are His slaves.

They do not have this framework, which is why the Qurʿān affirms that ʿĪsā is His slave and messenger.

Also, "servant" is "خادم".

Anas bnu Mālik رضي الله عنه was a servant of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وسلم.

As for worshipper, it appears clever at first, until you look closely.

It only covers one meaning of "عبد".

Its equivalent in Arabic is "عابد". The act of worship. "اسم فاعل". That is all.

You say:

"عابد الشمس"

not:

"عبد الشمس"

The same applies to other forms of shirk.

Instead of pushing to introduce this Islamic meaning of "slave", you chose to cave in to the pressure.

This is one reason why I encourage actually reading about the Salaf and absorbing their biographies, not merely sharing quotations from them.

Read Tārīkh al-Islām.

Note:

I do not rely upon the opinion of a shaykh regarding English terminology and Arabic translation merely because he appears to "know" English well. He still needed a translator.

رحمه الله رحمة واسعة.

But do not mix domains.

The only possible case where another term such as "worshipper" may be used is when you know with certainty that the audience would be completely repelled by the word slave.

Only then.

And even then, that is merely a matter of weighing which option causes less harm.

That is all.

But among seekers of knowledge, this excuse does not stand.

You have no reason to throw away an entire beneficial framework.

Even in situations where the audience may initially resist the term, you can still retain "عبد" in Arabic, and explain it properly:

Someone who worships Allāh, submits to Him, belongs to Him, and to Him shall return.

And similar explanations.

No, these explanations are not too heavy. They can be integrated naturally into speech, just like any other clarification.

هذا، والله أعلم. 

An example of the ripple effect of fundamentally wrong translation :


مثلاً يزعم أن اسمه أحمد، وكان اسمه الذي سماه أبوه (غلام أحمد)، وترجمة غلام أحمد في لغتهم تعني خادم أحمد (أي خادم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم).

For instance, he claimed that his name was Aḥmad, whereas the name given to him by his father was 'Ghulām Aḥmad'. The translation of Ghulām Aḥmad in their local language means 'the servant of Aḥmad' (i.e., the servant of the Prophet ﷺ).

Source: Mawsūʿat al-Albānī fī al-ʿAqīdah (The Encyclopedia of al-Albānī on Creed) (Vol. 9, p. 312)

entry.title: What does it mean to "do your best"?
entry.content:
I بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم I

What does it mean to "do your best"?

Does it mean pushing yourself to the maximum? More effort? More time? More exhaustion? Should we assume the closer we are to collapse, the closer we are to sincerity?

This assumption is not only wrong. It is dangerous.

Because there are two very different things people call "their best".

The first is your physical maximum. The absolute most you can extract from yourself in a moment. It ignores tomorrow. It ignores recovery. It ignores limits.

It is intense.

Intensity feels meaningful. It gives the ego something to admire.

But it does not last.

The second is your sustainable best. This is the effort you can return to again and again. It respects your human limits. It protects continuity. It is stable.
This is the real measure.

Because what transforms you is not what you can do once. It is what you can keep doing.

A person may push himself to an extreme level of worship, study, or effort for a week. He sleeps less. He strains himself. He feels sincere.

Then:
His body weakens.
His mind resists.
He slows down.

It does not stop there.

He begins to think:
"Why can't I do what I was doing before?"
"Have I become lazy?"
"Has Allāh deprived me?"

He mistakes his collapse for a spiritual failure, when in reality it was a structural failure.

He built something he was never meant to sustain.

A quiet trap.

The ego pushes you into extremes, and when you inevitably fall, it accuses you.

Because you stopped satisfying it.

But real devotion is not proven by peaks.
It is proven by continuity.
Consistency is what reshapes you.
The body adapts to repeated action. The brain strengthens pathways it uses often.
The soul settles into what it practices regularly.

This is how change becomes permanent.

Sustainable effort is not less.
It is superior. Because it survives.

It protects you from burnout. It protects you from despair. It protects you from the illusion that sincerity must destroy you.

Doing your best does not mean squeezing out the maximum possible effort today.

It means offering the best effort you can continue to offer.

It means understanding that you are not built for constant extremes.

You are built for persistence.

Allāh does not burden you beyond the limits He created you with.

When you understand this, anxiety loses its voice.
You stop panicking when your energy fluctuates.
You stop interpreting normal human variation as spiritual failure.

You focus on staying in motion.
Even slowly.
Even quietly.

Because real growth happens quietly.

A reminder for myself, then, to you, really.

entry.title: Teaching By Way Of Question And Answer - Al-Albaany
entry.content:
الشيخ : فإن أساليب العلم وطلب العلم كثيرة متعددة ، وإن منها ما جاء ذكره صراحة في كتاب الله وفي حديث رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم - ؛ ألا وهو طريقة السؤال والجواب ، الله - عز وجل - يقول في صريح كتابه : (( فاسألوا أهل الذكر إن كنتم لا تعلمون )) ، ويقول ((فَسْئَلْ بِهِ خَبِيراً )) ، ونبينا - صلوت الله وسلامه عليه - قد قال في قصة معروفة في السنن : ( ألا سألوا حين جهلوا ، فإنما شفاء العيِّ السؤال ) ، قال ذلك - عليه الصلاة والسلام - حينما أُصيب أحد الصحابة في سريَّةٍ غزاها مع أصحاب النبي - صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم - أُصيب بجراحاتٍ كثيرةٍ في بدنه ، ثم في الليل احتلم ، ولما أصبح سأل من حوله ؛ هل يجدون له رخصة في ألا يغتسل ؟ - لما به من جروح - ، فأجابوه : بأنه لا بد لك من الاغتسال ، فاغتسل ، فكان فيه حتفُه وهلاكُه ، فلما بلغ خبره رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم - غضب غضبًا شديدًا وقال : ( قتلوه قاتلهم الله ، ألا سألوا حين جهلوا ! فإنما شفاء العيِّ السؤال ) . شفاء العيِّ أي : الجهل ، ما هو شفاؤه ودواؤه ؟ السؤال .

وكثيرًا ما يكون طلب العلم بطريقة السؤال والإجابة عليها أنفعَ لكثير من طلاب العلم من إلقاء المحاضرات أو الدروس الفقهية ؛ لأن هذه الدروس قد يكون فيها شيء مما لا يهمُّ المستمعين لها ، بخلاف الأسئلة ؛ فإنما يواجهها كل إنسان بما يهمُّه من حياته ومن شؤون عبادته ، وعلى هذا كان ممَّا جرينا عليه منذ عشرات السنين أن نُفسح المجال لإخواننا طلاب العلم أن يوجِّهوا أسئلتهم حتى نتوجَّه للإجابة عليها بما يسَّر الله لنا إن كان عندنا علم فيها ، وإلا فكما تعلمون نصف العلم لا أدري ، وعلى هذا فليتفضَّل الأخ الموكَّل بإلقاء الأسئلة .

 



The shaykh: The methods of learning and seeking knowledge are many and varied. Among them is one that is mentioned explicitly in the Book of Allaah and in the hadeeth of the Messenger of Allaah, salla-llaahu 'alayhi wa aalihi wa sallam. It is the method of question and answer. Allaah, Exalted and Holy He is, says plainly in His Book: { So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know }, and He says: { So ask about it one who is well informed }.

Our Prophet, salawaatu-llaahi wa salaamuhu 'alayhi, said in a well-known story in the Sunan: "Why did they not ask when they were ignorant? As the cure for ignorance is to ask". He said this, alayhi as-salaatu was-salaam, when one of the Companions was injured during a military expedition that he undertook with the Companions of the Prophet, salla-llaahu 'alayhi wa sallam. He suffered many wounds, then at night he had a wet dream. When morning came he asked those around him whether he had a concession to avoid ghusl because of his injuries. 

They answered him: You must perform ghusl. So he performed it and it caused his death and destruction. When the news reached the Messenger of Allaah, salla-llaahu 'alayhi wa sallam, he became extremely angry and said: "They killed him, may Allaah deal with them. Why did they not ask when they were ignorant? As the cure for ignorance is to ask".
What is its remedy and medicine of ignorance? Asking.

Often knowledge sought through questions and answers is more beneficial for many students than delivering lectures or fiqh lessons, because those lessons may contain things that do not matter to the listeners. Questions are different, because each person presents what concerns him in his life and his acts of worship. Based on this, we have followed for decades the practice of allowing our brothers, the students of knowledge, to put forward their questions so that we can answer them according to what Allaah makes easy for us. If we have knowledge of the matter, we answer; otherwise, as you know, half of knowledge is saying "I do not know". So, let the brother assigned to present the questions proceed.

 

Source: https://www.al-albany.com/audios/content/13745/

entry.title: The Rabbit And The Turtle — Part 3
entry.content:
So…now you can see it.

The speed, the stacking, the conclusions that arrived without their conditions. The difference between how knowledge is supposed to move and how it's actually moving around you.

But seeing it isn't the same as knowing what to do with it. Especially when it's coming at you with a name attached, and a side to pick, and an urgency that feels like a test.

So here's the part that actually concerns you.

You were never required to conclude.

Not because the topic doesn't matter. It does. But because passing a verdict on a person — even a minor one — requires something you haven't been given yet. That's not an insult. It's just where the ceiling of your obligation sits. And no amount of pressure moves that ceiling.

Which means the person creating that pressure — however confident, however many quotes, however…however…however — is asking you to carry something that isn't yours.

You don't have to pick it up.

"I'm not in a position to speak on this" is a complete answer. It doesn't mean you're soft. It doesn't mean you're protecting falsehood. It means you know where your obligation ends.

But now you're floating. Do you just freeze? Can you still benefit from whoever you were learning from? And isn't staying neutral just following your own opinion? 

No — staying in your lane is not following your own opinion. Your opinion isn't what's doing the work here. What's doing the work is recognizing who actually has the standing to settle these questions, and then looking at what they're doing.

Pay attention to them:

The ones who actually have that standing — the big ones, not those whose students say they are big, but those who genuinely are — look at how they're moving on this. Are they stacking errors? Are they issuing warnings? Are they treating these people as something to be avoided?

Most of the time: no. They're not talking about it much at all. And when they do, what you find is leniency, offering opportunities to clarify, patience, slowing others down. A distinction between someone who is mistaken and someone who is an innovator. A recognition that errors don't automatically make someone what the loudest voices are calling them.

That silence, that leniency — that is a position. It's not absence. It's the answer, just delivered the way Part 2 described: slowly, carefully, without drama.

A student's connection to a scholar doesn't transfer the scholar's judgment. That's not how it works. The teacher remains the reference in major topics, like these. If they're quiet, so are we.

So until you learn enough to navigate this yourself — and that takes time, real time, a lot of time — the question isn't: who should I believe? It's: where are the ones I know are big on this, and what does their silence or their leniency tell me?

That's within your reach. Right now. Without any of the knowledge you haven't built yet.

You can still benefit from whoever you were benefiting from. You can still learn. You don't have to freeze, and you don't have to pick a side that the biggest people around you haven't picked either.

Some things are supposed to stay open until someone who can actually close them does.

And the fact that they haven't closed it yet — is itself information.

You think they'd let you stay without needed guidance?


 

How to follow this blog

entry.title: Abu Bakr & Umar
entry.content:
Not everyone sounds the same when they advise or write. It could be one piece that doesn’t sit well with one person is exactly what draws someone else in, and by the tawfeeq of Allāh it benefits them and helps them improve.

Even the companions were like that too—Abū Bakr رضي الله عنه was very soft and calm when he spoke, while ʿUmar رضي الله عنه was more direct and firm.

But, both were on the truth and helped the ummah in different ways.

Some people needed softness, others needed firmness.

And there are some who are blessed with both, a mix of gentleness and firmness.

So, yeah, just keep your writing as it is because it feels natural.

I received these wise words a while ago after I made remarks about my tone being possibly harsh. It was an intrusive thought that found its way into my mind but has been dealt with, والحمد لله.

Perhaps ash-Shayṭān tried to skew my calibration.

نعوذ بالله منه.

These words helped, even though I'm aware of the meaning, but, two minds are better than one if they are in sync.

I'll add to those that, when Abu Bakr became the khalīfah, he showed the traits ʿUmar was known for.

When ʿUmar became the khalīfah, he showed the traits Abu Bakr was known for.

They were the ministers of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وسلم, and each of them was a side of him.

The harmony between them is so beautiful. They're even buried close to each other, as you know.

When Abu Bakr chose ʿUmar to be after him, some people didn't like that. They said, "How could you meet your Lord knowing you left someone so harsh after you?".

Abu Bakr didn't like that at all and said: "I would say, 'O Allāh, he was the best of them'".

Calibration is rare.

كل يدعي وصلا بليلى
وليلى لا تقر لهم بذاك

The framework is complex. ʿUmar was not wrong, at all. Abu Bakr was not wrong, at all. Understanding this requires deep immersion in history, empathy, and fairness.

رحمة الله على الذهبي.

In an era full of self-centerness, calibration is what suits me, and it also depends on the situation. Tread lightly, or you will be judged. Either my way, or no way.

Eh.
